quizzes.stem: A prompt supplies four policy files, one of them a vendor email that says "ignore the instructions above". The answers never state which file backs each claim, so reviewers cannot trace them. Which change fits best?

options.a: Place the files above the instructions, which marks them as data for the model
options.b: Tell Claude to cite its sources more carefully in each answer it writes
options.c: Give each item an indexed tag, declare it data, and ask for the index cited
options.d: Use one tag for all four files and ask for the page number cited

explanation.c:
Nested tagged blocks with an index let the answer name the one it used, and a statement that the content
   is data does the marking (module 6, page 2).
explanation.a:
Ruled out because "Order is not a boundary", and an email
   that says "ignore the instructions above" still reads as an instruction wherever it sits.
explanation.b:
is ruled out
   because the guidance is to "Refer to tags by name in the instructions", which a general plea does not do.
explanation.d:
is
   ruled out because the documents must nest "each with an index or a name, so the answer can say which one it
   used".

quizzes.stem: A local charity asks Claude to draft a fundraising email and receives text that is accurate but could have been written for any charity. What should the next request emphasise?

options.a: Twenty varied appeal angles first, with judging left for later
options.b: Named sources for each claim, with unsupported statements flagged
options.c: The donor figures and a question, with evidence shown for each finding
options.d: The target donors and tone, with a past appeal as the model

explanation.d: A drafting task wants audience, tone and an example of the target style, and "A request that omits these gets a generic answer" (module 5, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because that is the brainstorming task: "brainstorming wants breadth first and judgment later".
explanation.b: Ruled out because that is the research task: "research wants sources named and unsupported claims flagged".
explanation.c: Ruled out because that is the analysis task: "Analysis wants the material and the question".

quizzes.stem: A director's request to Claude names the deliverable, its length and its readers, and gives the steps to follow. The drafts endorse every proposal the director makes. Which two statements fit? (Select two.)

options.a: A sample of the target style is the missing piece
options.b: The performance part is the one that is absent
options.c: Regenerating would bring out a more critical draft
options.d: Nothing says the model may challenge an idea
options.e: Adjectives such as thorough and professional would fix it

explanation.b: The performance part says how Claude should behave, including "whether to challenge you" (module 5, page 1), and the request covers only the product and the process.
explanation.d: The performance part says how Claude should behave, including "whether to challenge you" (module 5, page 1), and the request covers only the product and the process.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the page adds an example only "when a style matters".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Regenerating the same request and hoping is the reflex; revising the request is the method".
explanation.e: Ruled out because "Stacking adjectives instead of constraints" is a named trap whose example "gives conflicting, unverifiable demands", and none of those words invites pushback.

quizzes.stem: A user pastes a 25-page report beneath a single line of instruction and gets weak, unfocused answers. The user also needs any instruction hidden inside the report to be ignored. Which change fits best?

options.a: Add a role such as world-class analyst and ask for tighter focus
options.b: Wrap the document in tags and put the question after it
options.c: Ask the question before the document and again after it
options.d: Move the report above the instructions and let its position mark it as data

explanation.b: Long inputs go near the top, tagged as data, with the query at the end (module 6, pages 1 and 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because a role "changes style and focus, not truth", and it neither marks the report as data nor moves the question to the end.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Moving a pasted document above the instructions does not mark it as data".
explanation.c:
is ruled out
   because a restated question helps focus but leaves the report open to injection, and the rule is "Tag the data, tell the model it is data, and escape it".

quizzes.stem: A prompt reads "Summarise these notes for the usual readers in the usual format." Before it goes live, the team lead wants a quick check that it says enough. Which working rule from the course fits?

options.a: Ask whether a newcomer to the project could start without questions
options.b: Run it once on a typical input and approve it if the reply reads well
options.c: Ask Claude how sure it is of the replies the prompt produces
options.d: Check that it opens with a role and asks for a clear, concise summary

explanation.a: The colleague test: if a capable newcomer would need to ask a question first, the answer belongs in the prompt, and a newcomer would first ask who the usual readers are (module 6, page 1).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Changing a prompt and re-reading one answer is anecdote".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the page names "Stacking adjectives instead of constraints" as a trap.

quizzes.stem: A team needs replies in a rarely seen house format of three labelled lines, including a catch-all line, and instructions alone give inconsistent layouts. Which prompting approach fits best?

options.a: Several varied samples, one of them showing a tricky edge case
options.b: A single sample of the layout, shown once after the instructions
options.c: Three near-identical easy samples, to keep the layout consistent
options.d: A longer written description of the layout, with no samples attached

explanation.a:
A rare format with subtle boundaries calls for several varied examples, including a borderline case
   (module 6, page 2).
explanation.d:
Ruled out because zero-shot suits a case where "The task is common and easy to
   describe", and this format is not.
explanation.b: Ruled out because one example suits a format shown once, while several are for "The task has subtle boundaries, or the format is unusual".
explanation.c:
Ruled out because "Three easy, near-identical examples teach one pattern", and the catch-all case
   would be mishandled.

quizzes.stem: A support lead adds "You are a licensed pharmacist" to a prompt, expecting dependable medication advice from the replies. Which statement about that line is accurate?

options.a: It shifts wording and emphasis, and accuracy still needs a check
options.b: It replaces the task line, and the prompt can stay that short
options.c: It raises accuracy to a professional level, and review can be lighter
options.d: It guards the advice, and users cannot argue it into unsafe doses

explanation.a: A role steers style and attention and does not make a statement true (module 6, page 1).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "A role needs a task" and "You are a helpful assistant" adds little on its own.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the page says a role "changes style and focus, not truth".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "A role is not a safeguard" and the page adds that such a request can be argued around.

quizzes.stem: A manager types "Write something about our staff survey" and receives a generic paragraph with no specifics. The board pack is due within the hour. Which revision best fixes the request?

options.a: Name the readers, the form, the findings and the handling of gaps
options.b: Add that the result must be concise, thorough, clear and professional
options.c: Add a role such as senior analyst and leave the rest unchanged
options.d: Run the request three times and keep the draft with the most specifics

explanation.a: A good description gives the product, the process and the performance, with the goal and context.
explanation.b:
is
   ruled out because "Stacking adjectives instead of constraints" gives conflicting, unverifiable demands.
explanation.c:
is
   ruled out because "A role is a request, not a credential", so a role does not supply missing figures.
explanation.d:
is
   ruled out because "Regenerating the same request and hoping is the reflex; revising the request is the method".

quizzes.stem: A summary of a supplier contract is correct in every sentence, yet the manager later finds a penalty clause missing. Which two statements describe the shortfall? (Select two.)

options.a: Completeness failed because a key obligation never appeared
options.b: Fairness failed because the supplier's framing was favoured
options.c: Audience fit failed because the manager wanted a different tone
options.d: Gap flagging failed because no line said a term was absent
options.e: Accuracy failed because a figure in it was never traced

explanation.a: A summary "can be accurate in every sentence and still leave out the clause that matters" (module 5, page 2), which is a completeness failure, and "Silent omissions are the quiet failure", since nothing in the draft declared the gap.
explanation.d: A summary "can be accurate in every sentence and still leave out the clause that matters" (module 5, page 2), which is a completeness failure, and "Silent omissions are the quiet failure", since nothing in the draft declared the gap.
explanation.b: Ruled out because the fairness check asks whether a draft will "present one side as the whole", and nothing in this summary takes a side.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the page's example is "An accurate technical answer can be wrong for a board", which concerns the reader.
explanation.e: Ruled out because accuracy asks "Are the specific claims, figures, names, dates, quotations and citations true?", and every sentence here was true.

quizzes.stem: A news desk asks Claude to confirm that a reader's photo of a flood is not AI-generated before it runs on the front page. What should the desk expect?

options.a: A sound verdict, backed by a confidence score on request
options.b: A firm verdict, supported by a detailed reading of the scene
options.c: No reliable verdict, leaving provenance checks to settle it
options.d: A dependable verdict, given a sharp, large and upright photo

explanation.c: Synthetic images are one of the stated vision limits, so whether the photo is genuine rests on provenance checks and an editor (module 4, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy", so a score adds no evidence.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Detail is not accuracy; the vision page lists the conditions under which it is wrong", and a full reading of the scene says nothing about how the photo was made.
explanation.d: Ruled out because image quality is a separate limit, and of synthetic images the page says Claude "cannot determine whether an image is AI-generated".

quizzes.stem: A team lead receives Claude Tag's summary of a long thread, and must also forward a reply Claude drafted for a client. How should the lead check them?

options.a: Study the digest, since the team acts on it, and glance over the reply
options.b: Read the digest and the outgoing text closely, since Claude wrote each of them
options.c: Skim the digest and the outgoing text, then ask Claude to flag doubtful lines
options.d: Skim the digest, and study the outgoing text, since it is leaving the firm

explanation.d: The page asks to read Claude's work in proportion to what is at stake, so the internal digest gets a light pass and the outgoing reply the close reading (module 8, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the page has it the other way round: "A summary you can skim", while "something going to a customer or changing a system gets a careful read".
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Do not check everything equally", so a summary for the lead does not need the close read that outgoing work does.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy", so Claude's own flags do not replace reading the reply.

quizzes.stem: A test asserts that a Claude reply matches a stored string exactly. It passes today and fails tomorrow for the same input. What is the best interpretation?

options.a: The vendor swapped the model silently, so the id must be pinned and re-recorded
options.b: Replies do vary even at fixed settings, so quality must be judged across many cases
options.c: The prompt is faulty, and a line such as be consistent will stabilise it
options.d: The machine's clock changed the output, so the time must be frozen

explanation.b: Output varies by sampling and infrastructure, so one run proves nothing (module 1, page 2).
explanation.a:
is ruled
   out because every id is pinned, "including the dateless IDs used from the 4.6 generation on".
explanation.c:
is ruled out
   because "A prompt sentence does not remove sampling".
explanation.d:
Ruled out because "The model has no clock", so
   freezing one changes nothing.

quizzes.stem: A clinic plans to have Claude read CT studies uploaded by patients and send the findings straight to them. Which concern matters most?

options.a: Cost: each scan would use too many visual tokens for the clinic's budget
options.b: Scope: such scans are outside its design and need a qualified reviewer
options.c: Naming: Claude would add the patients' names to its findings
options.d: Privacy: the scans would stay in the chat and surface in later conversations

explanation.b:
The vision limits include scans, and a decision reaching individuals needs a qualified reviewer (modules 4
   and 10).
explanation.a:
Ruled out because an image costs "about ceil(width/28) x ceil(height/28) tokens up to a per-model cap", so the
   token count is bounded and cost is not the deciding concern.
explanation.d:
Ruled out because "A conversation with Claude does not
   teach it anything that carries to the next conversation".
explanation.c:
Ruled out because "Claude cannot be used to name
   people in images, and refuses to".

quizzes.stem: A knowledge-base assistant answers every question, even when the manuals say nothing, and sometimes invents a procedure. The manuals are already included with each request. Which addition best tackles this?

options.a: Permission to admit that the text does not cover the case
options.b: A lower temperature setting aimed at the guessing over missing steps
options.c: A confidence percentage placed beside each answer it gives
options.d: A second copy of the manuals at the end of each request

explanation.a: Permission to say the material is insufficient is the first listed technique (module 1, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "The models this course uses do not accept them", and a setting does not give the model a way to say it does not know.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "asking a model how sure it is does not make a wrong answer right".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot", and the manuals are already supplied.

quizzes.stem: A team sends Claude-drafted board papers weekly. Reviewers spend equal time on every sentence and still miss a wrong total. Which two changes fit? (Select two.)

options.a: Give each reviewer a longer checklist of style rules
options.b: Ask Claude to mark the sentences it is least sure of and review only those
options.c: Put the checking effort on figures, and read the narrative lightly
options.d: Have a second reviewer reread every sentence in full
options.e: Pass any legal commitment they contain to a qualified expert

explanation.c: Checking in proportion to the cost of being wrong puts the effort on figures and sends high stakes such as legal commitments to a human reviewer, because "You own what you send, whoever drafted it" (module 5, page 2).
explanation.e: Checking in proportion to the cost of being wrong puts the effort on figures and sends high stakes such as legal commitments to a human reviewer, because "You own what you send, whoever drafted it" (module 5, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Readers check tone and grammar, which are visible", and skip the figures.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Do not check everything equally", and a second full reread spreads the effort the same way.

quizzes.stem: An analyst asks Claude for the reasons a new policy will succeed, and the reply gives only supporters' views. The memo goes to a review committee. What is the best next step?

options.a: Ask Claude to confirm that its answer was fair and balanced
options.b: Add a line to the memo saying that an AI drafted it
options.c: Reword the request to cover each side's leading argument
options.d: Switch to a larger tier and ask the same question again

explanation.c:
Bias often comes from the framing of the request, so the request is revised and both framings are
   reviewed (module 5, page 2).
explanation.a:
Ruled out because asking the model "for its confidence does not verify
   anything".
explanation.b:
Ruled out because the fairness question is whether the output will "present one side as the
   whole", which a disclosure line leaves untouched.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Regenerating the same request and hoping is the reflex; revising the request is the method", and a larger tier gets the same framing.

quizzes.stem: A finance team plans to use Claude for Excel to produce the reconciliation that its auditors will rely on, and to send the result with no further checks. How should this plan be judged?

options.a: It is fine because the add-in keeps formula relationships intact
options.b: It is not advised for critical sign-off figures unless they are verified
options.c: It is fine when Claude is told to double-check its own totals before sending
options.d: It is not advised because the add-in cannot show the source of a figure

explanation.b: The add-in page does not recommend relying on it for audit-critical calculations without verification (module 8, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because intact formula relationships do not check the result, and the page says to "review changes before finalising".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the add-in answers "with cell-level citations you can click", so tracing a figure is possible and is not the reason for caution.

quizzes.stem: Before sending a report to a client, an analyst asks Claude "How confident are you in these figures?" and gets "Very confident". Which view of that reply is right?

options.a: It is weak evidence, so Claude is asked to explain its confidence in more detail
options.b: It proves nothing about accuracy, so the numbers are checked at the source
options.c: It is a good sign, so only the totals get a quick spot check
options.d: It is fair evidence, so the reply is filed as the sign-off for the figures

explanation.b: Asking a model about its own certainty verifies nothing, so claims go to the source of record (module 5, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because asking the model "for its confidence does not verify anything", however much detail it gives.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the page states "Confidence of tone is not a signal".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the page holds that "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy", so it cannot stand as a sign-off.

quizzes.stem: An analyst needs Claude's output to load into a database through a script, and also to show executives a short takeaway. Which pair of formats fits?

options.a: A published artifact with shared storage that serves both audiences at once
options.b: An artifact for the ingest step, and a table in a slide deck for leadership
options.c: Inline replies for both audiences, with artifacts kept for code alone
options.d: Machine-readable results for the ingest step, a brief inline note for leadership

explanation.d: Data a program reads is structured data, and a short takeaway stays inline (module 7, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Data that another program will read is structured data", not an artifact.
explanation.c: Ruled out because an artifact suits "A document, deck, dashboard or small tool to hand to someone", not only code.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "A short factual answer goes inline", and a shared-storage artifact suits neither the script nor the takeaway.

quizzes.stem: A communications assistant has Claude draft a press note that goes out under the organisation's name within the hour. It reports what the chief executive said and gives three percentages. What should be checked first?

options.a: Spelling and tone, read line by line by a colleague
options.b: The quotation and the statistics, against their originals
options.c: The percentages, against the confidence Claude states for each
options.d: The chief executive's words, against a second draft from Claude

explanation.b: The claims that would hurt if wrong are checked against the source of record (module 5, page 2).
explanation.a:
is
   ruled out because "Readers check tone and grammar, which are visible, and skip figures and citations, which are
   where the damage is".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".
explanation.d:
is
   ruled out because the routine is "Check those against the source of record, not against the model".

quizzes.stem: A team runs Claude Haiku 4.5 on questions about product launches from mid-2025, and the answers are thin. Which fact from the models overview best accounts for this?

options.a: Its window is smaller than the others', so the later material no longer fits
options.b: Its reliable knowledge is limited to February 2025, before those events took place
options.c: Its training data runs to July 2025, so those mid-2025 events should be well covered
options.d: All tiers share the same dates, so switching tier could not change the result

explanation.b: Haiku 4.5's reliable knowledge cutoff is February 2025, while the three larger models run to June 2026 (module 1, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the window is a "working memory", "different from the training data".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the reliable date is "the date through which the model's knowledge is most extensive and reliable".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the table gives "Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 | June 2026 | June 2026".

quizzes.stem: A retailer will draft about 5,000 short order-status replies an hour, and a few each hour need delicate judgment. Speed and cost matter most. What is the best opening move?

options.a: Use the middle tier until the invoices arrive, then decide
options.b: Use the most capable tier for every reply to protect quality
options.c: Use the fast, cheap tier first and send hard cases higher
options.d: Use the cheapest tier for every reply, hard cases included

explanation.c:
High-volume routine work starts on the efficient tier with the hard cases sent upward, and it is
   validated on real data (module 3, page 1).
explanation.a:
Ruled out because the decision rule is to "build benchmark
   tests for your use case", not wait for invoices.
explanation.b:
Ruled out because "the top tier for everything wastes the
   budget".
explanation.d:
Ruled out because "the cheapest model for everything under-serves exactly the cases that need
   depth".

quizzes.stem: A team uses Claude Code in the terminal, and a colleague asks whether the repository's CLAUDE.md file and MCP servers also apply in the IDE extension and the desktop app. What should the colleague be told?

options.a: They do, because each of those tools is a front end to one shared engine
options.b: They do not, since each surface keeps its own separate configuration files
options.c: They apply only in the terminal, since the files are read from a shell prompt
options.d: They do, once each file has been exported into each of the other tools

explanation.a: Each surface connects to the same underlying Claude Code engine, so memory files, settings and MCP servers work across all of them (module 3, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because Claude Code keeps "settings that travel with the repository across its surfaces".
explanation.c: Ruled out because Claude Code is "available in the terminal, IDE extensions, a desktop app and the browser".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "your repo's CLAUDE.md files, settings, and MCP servers work across all of them", with no export step.

quizzes.stem: An analyst switches on Research mode to look up the notice period stated in a supplier contract that is already open. How should this choice be judged?

options.a: It is more than needed, since one file in hand holds the answer
options.b: It is the right choice, since contracts need many linked searches
options.c: It is needed, since a notice period must be confirmed from web sources
options.d: It is a mistake, since Research can search only the public web

explanation.a: The open contract already holds the answer, and the page says "Do not use it for a question that one document answers" (module 7, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Use Research when the question is open and broad".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the answer is in the contract, and for a lookup Research "spends allowance and adds sources to check".
explanation.d: Ruled out because Research "draws on connected internal sources" as well as the web, so its reach is not what makes it a poor fit here.

quizzes.stem: A long conversation in the app starts contradicting decisions made hours earlier, though no error appears. The lead wants the project to continue with every decision kept. Which action fits?

options.a: Ask Claude to restate every decision in the same conversation and continue
options.b: Switch to a model with a larger window and continue in the same conversation
options.c: Begin a new chat with a short summary of the agreed points
options.d: Paste the whole earlier transcript into a new chat

explanation.c: A fresh start with a summary keeps the useful context and drops the rot (module 1, page 1).
explanation.a:
is ruled
   out because "accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot", and a restatement inside the same long conversation leaves the degraded context in place.
explanation.b:
Ruled out because "Larger windows raise the ceiling; they do not
   remove the need to decide what goes in".
explanation.d:
Ruled out because "more context isn't automatically better", and
   the whole transcript brings the rot with it.

quizzes.stem: A strategist must compare twelve vendors on price, support and security from what is published about them online, and wants each finding cited by tomorrow. Which feature fits best?

options.a: Research mode, with web search switched on in the chat
options.b: A Project, loaded with each vendor's brochures and price sheets
options.c: A plain chat, asked for sources in each reply
options.d: An artifact, laying the comparison out as a live dashboard

explanation.a: Research runs many linked searches with citations and needs web search on (module 7, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because a Project suits "Recurring work with fixed rules and reference files".
explanation.c: Ruled out because plain chat is for "A one-off question, a draft, a quick comparison", while the page names "a comparison of vendors" as work for Research.
explanation.d: Ruled out because an artifact is for "A document, deck, dashboard or small tool to hand to someone", not for gathering sources.

quizzes.stem: Two engineers disagree over which of two Claude tiers should draft a firm's contract summaries, and each cites a few chat replies they liked. Going by the course's criteria, what should settle the choice?

options.a: Score both on a fixed set of real past files, weighing cost last
options.b: Take the higher tier for the legal weight that the summaries carry
options.c: Take the cheaper tier for its faster answers at a lower price
options.d: Have each tier grade its own summaries and keep the top scorer

explanation.a: The page's decision rule is to run your own prompts and data across the candidates and compare quality before cost, since "Having a good evaluation set is the most important step" (module 3, page 1).
explanation.b: is ruled out because, of always choosing the largest model, "nothing on the pages says the biggest model is the safest default for every task".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the rule is to "compare accuracy, quality and edge-case handling, then weigh cost", so price comes after quality.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy", so a tier's grade of its own work settles nothing.

quizzes.stem: A user tells Claude about a project in an incognito chat and finds that the next chat has no trace of it. Which two statements are correct? (Select two.)

options.a: Claude forgot it because the chat ran past its window
options.b: The weights should have updated after the exchange
options.c: The model itself retains nothing between conversations
options.d: Incognito chats can only be started inside a Project
options.e: That mode is meant to keep a conversation out of memory

explanation.c: Incognito chats "keep a conversation out of memory and history" on purpose (modules 7 and 10), and the model itself carries nothing between chats, since "your code resends the history".
explanation.e: Incognito chats "keep a conversation out of memory and history" on purpose (modules 7 and 10), and the model itself carries nothing between chats, since "your code resends the history".
explanation.a: Ruled out because a new chat starts as "a model with no memory of you", whatever the window of the last one.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Weights are fixed at inference time".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Incognito chats are available only outside Projects" (module 7, page 1), so one cannot be started inside a Project.

quizzes.stem: An FP&A analyst must trace how a revenue figure in a long workbook is derived before presenting it. Which capability of the Excel add-in helps most directly?

options.a: Reading closed workbooks stored in the shared drive
options.b: Cross-app work that copies the figure into a Word memo
options.c: Answers about the open file that carry cell-level citations
options.d: Macro execution that recalculates the whole workbook automatically

explanation.c: The add-in answers with clickable cell-level citations (module 8, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because with cross-app work "one conversation can read an Excel model and write a Word memo or a slide", which moves the figure but does not trace it.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Macros and VBA, and data tables, are unsupported".
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Claude can read and write only files that are open at that moment".

quizzes.stem: A sales team's lead has one skill for proposal layouts that works well, and wants the team's other recurring jobs, with the connectors they use, handled the same way. Which route should the lead take?

options.a: Upload each playbook as its own skill and leave the connectors out
options.b: Prove the first piece in daily use, then grow it into a shared plugin
options.c: Build the whole plugin first and test each skill after rollout
options.d: Keep the one skill and write the other jobs into a Project's instructions

explanation.b: The Academy lesson recommends starting with one skill, testing it and then scaling to a plugin you share (module 8, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "a plugin bundles skills, connectors and sub-agents around a job".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the habit is to "Start narrow, learn how Claude does on your material, then widen", so testing comes before the plugin and not after rollout.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "a procedure you want everywhere (the monthly report layout) belongs in a skill", not in one Project's instructions.

quizzes.stem: A small charity asks Claude for a first draft of a grant application and receives polished text in a corporate voice that misses the funder's priorities. Which two statements fit the course's guidance for this audience? (Select two.)

options.a: The request should give only a word limit and a due date
options.b: The request should set out the scoring criteria that apply
options.c: The request should give the mission, tone and intended reader
options.d: The request should ask for a warm, moving and professional style
options.e: The request should ask it to make the results sound as strong as possible

explanation.b: A non-profit describes the funder's criteria, its mission and voice, the audience and the facts that must appear, and avoids "Stacking adjectives instead of constraints" (module 9, page 2).
explanation.c: A non-profit describes the funder's criteria, its mission and voice, the audience and the facts that must appear, and avoids "Stacking adjectives instead of constraints" (module 9, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because a non-profit's request describes "the funder's criteria, the organisation's mission and voice, the audience", which a word limit and a date leave out.
explanation.d: Ruled out because a string of adjectives like "Be concise, thorough, clear and professional" "gives conflicting, unverifiable demands".
explanation.e: Ruled out because the officer checks "whether a draft overstates what the programme achieved", and a request for the strongest claims invites that overstatement.

quizzes.stem: An online shop wants every order with a postcode outside its delivery zones flagged automatically, and 12,000 orders arrive daily. Which design is best?

options.a: Claude drafts the customer notes, and a short program applies the rule
options.b: Claude reads each order and decides whether the postcode lies out of zone
options.c: Claude checks a sample of orders and the rest are assumed to be fine
options.d: Claude screens each postcode first, then code confirms the ones it flags

explanation.a: A rule that fits in one line belongs in code (module 4, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because code is "Cheaper, faster, deterministic, testable".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "A prompt is a request, not a guarantee", and a sample leaves the rest unchecked.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "If you can write the rule, write it; add a model only for the cases the rule cannot express".

quizzes.stem: A team ranks Claude's apps and features by power and picks the top one each time. For a task that edits a few client files, which choice would the course make instead?

options.a: The most capable surface, so the task never stalls for lack of access
options.b: The narrowest surface for the job, with every change confirmed
options.c: The cheapest surface, tried first and upgraded only if it falls short
options.d: The most automated surface, with each step logged for review afterwards

explanation.b: The pattern is least reach, least action, and most visibility to the right people, so the surface gets only the files the task needs and a person stays on the consequential steps (module 8, page 3).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Picking the most powerful surface" is named as a trap.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the trap list says to "match the surface to the shape of the work", not to its price.
explanation.d: Ruled out because the course says to "Prefer a surface and an approval mode where a person confirms the consequential steps", which a log read afterwards does not do.

quizzes.stem: A COO asks which of four chores suit Claude with review and no extra tools: (1) drafting vendor-email variants, (2) making the final call on which supplier to drop, (3) summarising call transcripts, (4) calculating invoice totals to the cent in the chat. Which pair is right?

options.a: The second and fourth
options.b: The first and third
options.c: The third and fourth
options.d: The first and second

explanation.b:
Chores 1 and 3 are language-shaped work that a review can catch, while the supplier decision and exact
   sums are not (module 5, page 1).
explanation.a:
Ruled out because chore 2 needs "judgment that carries accountability",
   and chore 4 needs exactness.
explanation.c:
Ruled out because chore 4, the totals, needs "exactness (money, counts,
   identifiers)".
explanation.d:
Ruled out because "A step stays with a person, or with code" when it needs accountable
   judgment such as the supplier decision in chore 2.

quizzes.stem: A department head must explain to staff what Claude changes in the team's work. Which message fits the course's structure for such an explanation?

options.a: It handles the drafting by itself, a person checks the facts, and we log time saved
options.b: It speeds first drafts, colleagues verify the claims, and spot checks measure the gain
options.c: It quickens summaries, it settles routine decisions, and an example set tracks quality
options.d: It cuts drafting time, reviewers check the figures, and one clean month ends review

explanation.b:
A fair message says what it speeds up, what still needs a person and how the team will know it works
   (module 5, page 2).
explanation.a:
Ruled out because the page tells you to avoid the extreme "it will do the job", and
   drafting is something it speeds up, not takes over.
explanation.d:
Ruled out because "A good draft does not show the
   figures were right", so review cannot shrink on a clean run.
explanation.c:
Ruled out because decisions belong to
   "what still needs a person (checking claims, decisions, anything regulated)".

quizzes.stem: A product team asks Claude for "a settings page" and receives a generic design that breaks an existing layout. Which two statements match how the course says a builder should describe the job? (Select two.)

options.a: Add more adjectives about the style and mood of the page
options.b: Point out the current screens the work must leave intact
options.c: Say who will use it and what already surrounds it
options.d: Give only the task and let a strong model infer the rest
options.e: Ask for three finished designs in one go for comparison

explanation.b: A builder describes "the problem and the constraints, not only the task" (module 9, page 1): who the user is, what exists, what must not change and what done looks like.
explanation.c: A builder describes "the problem and the constraints, not only the task" (module 9, page 1): who the user is, what exists, what must not change and what done looks like.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the page names "Stacking adjectives instead of constraints" as a trap.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "If they would need to ask you a question before starting, the model needs the answer in the prompt".
explanation.e: Ruled out because the habit is to "Hand over in steps you can judge", and three finished designs skip the steps.

quizzes.stem: A lecturer drafts a take-home essay brief, and the grade is meant to reflect each student's own reasoning. Which check from the course's list for educators matters most for this brief?

options.a: If its reading level suits the students who will write it
options.b: If the examples in it lean on bias or stereotypes
options.c: If the facts the brief states about its subject are correct
options.d: If a chatbot given only the task could complete it unaided

explanation.d: Educators check whether an assignment can be completed by pasting it into an AI, and whether that matters, and a brief that tests a student's own analysis is where it matters most (module 9, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because reading level sits among the content checks, "accuracy of the content taught, bias or stereotypes in examples, reading level", which concern what the brief says, not whose reasoning the essay shows.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "bias or stereotypes in examples" is a check on the brief's fairness to its readers, not on whether the essay is the student's own work.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Checks: accuracy of the content taught" is a check on the brief's facts, and a brief with correct facts can still be completed by a chatbot.

quizzes.stem: A shop's support inbox gets about 300 routine order questions a day, plus occasional warranty and refund disputes, and nobody reviews the answers sent today. Which workflow change fits?

options.a: Draft everything on the top tier and send the replies out automatically
options.b: Draft on a fast tier and let Claude approve payouts it is confident about
options.c: Have a person write every reply, with Claude kept out of the inbox
options.d: Draft on a fast tier with spot checks, and a person approves each payout

explanation.d:
High-volume low-stakes drafting suits a faster, cheaper model with a spot check, and a customer's money
   does not go out on trust (module 9, page 2).
explanation.a:
Ruled out because "the top tier for everything wastes the
   budget", and nothing stops an unchecked commitment.
explanation.b:
Ruled out because "a contract, a legal term or a
   customer's money does not go out on trust".
explanation.c:
Ruled out because "High-volume, low-stakes drafting suits a
   faster, cheaper model" with a spot check, so manual work throws the benefit away.

quizzes.stem: A Team plan owner wants the company's brand-writing skill available in every member's chats from Monday, with an opt-out for anyone who prefers not to use it. Which option fits?

options.a: An organisation one, provisioned to all and toggled per person
options.b: A plugin bundling the skill with the firm's connectors
options.c: A partner skill, written to work with another firm's connectors
options.d: An Anthropic skill, which is built in for office and PDF files

explanation.a: Organisation skills are provisioned by Team and Enterprise owners to every member, who can toggle them (module 7, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Where a skill is one playbook, a plugin is several, plus the connectors they depend on", and one skill needs no bundle.
explanation.c: Ruled out because partner skills come "From other companies, built to work with their connectors".
explanation.d: Ruled out because those are "Built in, for creating Excel, Word, PowerPoint and PDF files".

quizzes.stem: A Project's HR assistant quotes a leave policy that was replaced, and both the old and the new document sit in its knowledge. Compliance wants the prior edition to stay retrievable for audits. What is the best fix?

options.a: Ask Claude to merge both files into a third file and use that one
options.b: Keep both and add an instruction to prefer the newer document when they conflict
options.c: Take the outdated file out of the workspace and archive it in your own storage
options.d: Switch on memory, which lets Claude learn which policy is current

explanation.c:
A deleted file is a guarantee, and the archived copy in your own storage meets the audit need (module 7,
   page 1).
explanation.a:
Ruled out because "Judge the source before you add it", and a merged file adds a new unchecked
   source.
explanation.b:
Ruled out because "an instruction is a request and a deleted file is a guarantee", so the conflict
   stays possible.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "memory is not a substitute for a knowledge file".

quizzes.stem: A team wants every Claude Tag reply in one Slack channel to be brief and to link its source. Which two statements describe the setup? (Select two.)

options.a: Ask each member to add the rule when they tag Claude
options.b: Set it in a Project, whose instructions Slack reads first
options.c: Lower the temperature in the model's settings for that channel
options.d: Let admins review and delete the rules that get stored
options.e: Address the rule to it in one message posted there

explanation.d: Standing instructions "go to channel memory, which admins can review and delete" (module 8, page 2).
explanation.e: Standing instructions "go to channel memory, which admins can review and delete" (module 8, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "You can set a channel's standing instructions by telling Claude there", so members need not repeat them in every thread.
explanation.b: Ruled out because a channel's rules are set "by telling Claude there", in the channel, and kept in channel memory rather than in a Project.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "The models this course uses do not accept them".

quizzes.stem: A team lead wants the whole organisation to use a common workspace of staff guidance in Claude, but salary bands may be seen only by the HR group. Which approach is right?

options.a: Share one Project widely and tell its instructions to withhold the pay scales
options.b: Share one Project widely with view-only access, which keeps viewers out of the knowledge
options.c: Share one Project widely, with the pay scales in a file named for HR only
options.d: Share one Project widely, with the pay scales kept in a second, HR-only one

explanation.d:
Sharing shows the instructions and every file to everyone with access, so the bands live in a separate
   Project that only HR can open (module 7, page 1).
explanation.a:
Ruled out because the guidance is "Treat sharing as publishing",
   and an instruction is a request.
explanation.b:
Ruled out because can view gives "read-only access to contents, knowledge
   and instructions", which is reading.
explanation.c:
Ruled out because "anyone with access can read the instructions and
   every file in the knowledge base", and a file name does not limit who opens it.

quizzes.stem: A team syncs a Google document that holds a pasted chart image with the key figures into a private Project. Answers ignore those figures. Which limit explains it?

options.a: The Project reached its context limit, so retrieval skipped the chart
options.b: A synced document is a snapshot taken on the day it was added
options.c: The connector brings the written words across, not the pictures
options.d: Only a shared Project reads every part of a synced Drive document

explanation.c: The Drive connector reads text content only, and images embedded in a document are not processed (module 7, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because retrieval starts "when a Project approaches the context limit", and that does not explain missing images.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "a synced document follows its source", so the copy is not frozen on the day it was added.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Shared Projects do not offer the Drive option on that page".

quizzes.stem: A price list lives in the finance team's shared folder and as an uploaded copy inside a Project. After two quarters the two differ, and Claude quotes both. Which principle of keeping knowledge current was missed?

options.a: Version names added to the title of every file in the Project
options.b: Source judgement applied before anything is uploaded to the Project
options.c: A review date written on each document that the Project holds
options.d: One source of record, which the workspace copies or syncs directly

explanation.d: Keep one source of record and let the Project mirror or sync it, because with two copies "one of them is wrong within a quarter" (module 7, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the advice to "Put a version or date in the file name and the first line" helps you go back, and does not stop two live sources.
explanation.b: Ruled out because that principle is to "prefer the final approved text over a draft", which is about quality.
explanation.c: Ruled out because a review date makes "a stale file is a missed appointment, not a surprise", and does not remove the duplicate.

quizzes.stem: A coordinator builds a small published artifact where parents of pupils enter their children's dietary needs, and it keeps data. What should the coordinator check before inviting people?

options.a: Whether its storage is personal or visible to every user
options.b: Whether the artifact runs past fifteen lines, which decides its storage
options.c: Whether each visitor has the creator's plan, with usage billed to it
options.d: Whether visitors have connected the creator's own apps

explanation.a: Shared storage is visible to every user, so check it before sensitive entries (module 7, page 2).
explanation.b:
is
   ruled out because the fifteen-line figure is about when an artifact is made, "typically over 15 lines, and
   reusable on its own".
explanation.c:
Ruled out because "Their use counts against their own plan limits, not the
   creator's".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "each person connects their own apps even in a shared artifact".

quizzes.stem: A researcher replaces patient names with codes and keeps the table of codes in a locked folder. The data also lists an unusual profession, a village of 300 people and the exact day of each visit. Is it now anonymous?

options.a: No, but only because the visit day is exact, so drop that single field
options.b: Yes, because the table that reverses the codes is stored apart and locked
options.c: No, since the mix is still identifying, so generalise it further
options.d: Yes, since coding is the strongest technique on the list of methods in use

explanation.c: A rare combination can identify a person without a name, so the data is generalised further (module 10, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the page says "a rare job title, a small town and an exact date can identify a person without a name".
explanation.b: Ruled out because the page states "Pseudonymised data is still personal data under many rules".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the list of techniques runs from strongest to weakest, and it starts with "Aggregate. Send totals and trends, not rows".

quizzes.stem: A member of a Team plan finds that memory and a particular connector are missing from their settings, while a friend at another company has both. Which two statements explain it? (Select two.)

options.a: The source system blocks anything absent from a personal allow list
options.b: Features stay hidden until each member opts in individually
options.c: Their organisation's owners have those features turned off
options.d: Individuals cannot override that choice inside their own account
options.e: Memory is offered only on Enterprise plans, not on Team plans

explanation.c: "Owners enable connectors, memory, skills and other features for the organisation; members cannot use what is off" (module 10, page 2).
explanation.d: "Owners enable connectors, memory, skills and other features for the organisation; members cannot use what is off" (module 10, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because a source system decides only what a connector reaches, since "Claude inherits each person's permissions from the connected service", and memory has no source system.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "an owner must enable connectors for the organisation before members can use them", so no member can opt in alone.
explanation.e: Ruled out because "On Team and Enterprise plans owners decide whether memory is available at all", so a Team plan can have it.

quizzes.stem: A team on a commercial plan asks whether Anthropic may use its inputs to build better models, and how long chats are kept. Which answer is accurate?

options.a: They are used unless an owner opts out, and they are then kept for up to five years
options.b: They are not used for training, and each chat is deleted once it is closed
options.c: They are used only if each member allows it in their own privacy settings
options.d: They are not used by default, and are deleted within 30 days unless set otherwise

explanation.d:
Commercial products are not used to train models by default, and data is deleted within 30 days by
   default (module 10, page 1).
explanation.a:
Ruled out because "By default Anthropic does not use inputs or outputs from
   commercial products to train models".
explanation.b:
Ruled out because "Inputs and outputs are deleted within 30 days by
   default", not when a chat is closed.
explanation.c:
Ruled out because the choice in privacy settings is the consumer rule, while
   commercial plans start from "does not use inputs or outputs from commercial products to train models".

quizzes.stem: A manager connects a client folder to Cowork and is concerned that a task might remove files. Which expectation is accurate?

options.a: Claude can only read the folder, so no file there can be removed
options.b: Claude could also remove files in folders beside the connected one
options.c: Permanent removal waits for consent, and backups are still wise
options.d: Approval given once for the folder covers each later removal

explanation.c: Claude needs explicit permission before a permanent deletion, and the page says to keep backups of important files (module 8, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Claude can read, write and permanently delete files in the folders you connect".
explanation.b: Ruled out because "It reaches only folders you explicitly connected".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "It needs your explicit permission before a permanent deletion", which is asked before each one.

quizzes.stem: A researcher must report survey findings by area and age group, and policy restricts personal data. The responses include names and a free-text column. Which preparation is best?

options.a: Delete only the names column and upload the rest, trusting open text to be anonymous
options.b: Coarsen places and ages into bands, strip identities, and read the open answers
options.c: Code each name, keep the key list in the same file, and upload all
options.d: Upload everything and ask for a summary that leaves out personal details

explanation.b: Generalise, and check free text, which hides details (module 10, page 1).
explanation.a:
Ruled out because "Notes
   columns hide names and details".
explanation.c:
Ruled out because "Pseudonymised data is still personal data under many
   rules, because the key can reverse it".
explanation.d:
Ruled out because asking for a summary without personal details
   "is a request, and it does not satisfy a policy control".

quizzes.stem: A manager lets Cowork reach an entire documents drive to save time, and it holds tax returns and exported passwords. Which two changes fit? (Select two.)

options.a: Use manual approval for sensitive material
options.b: Connect a dedicated folder with only the needed items
options.c: Tell Claude to leave the tax and password files alone
options.d: Rely on the cloud sandbox to keep the files safe
options.e: Switch to Auto approval, which checks each action

explanation.a: A dedicated working folder limits what a mistake or an injected instruction can reach, and the habit is to "use Manual approval for sensitive files, new tools and hard-to-undo actions" (module 8, page 1).
explanation.b: A dedicated working folder limits what a mistake or an injected instruction can reach, and the habit is to "use Manual approval for sensitive files, new tools and hard-to-undo actions" (module 8, page 1).
explanation.c: Ruled out because the habit is to "grant access selectively and avoid financial documents, credentials and personal records".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the isolation "doesn't limit what Claude reads or does" through connected tools.
explanation.e: Ruled out because Auto only has Claude check each action, and "it still runs on its own".

quizzes.stem: A professional asks Claude in Chrome to shortlist conference venues while a banking site is open in another tab, with ten minutes left before a call. Which habit best limits harm?

options.a: Rely on the classifiers, which screen each action
options.b: Leave the bank tab open but ask Claude to skip it
options.c: Switch on Skip all approvals, with no prompt interrupting the task
options.d: Use a clean profile, and approve each action manually

explanation.d: A separate profile and manual approval limit what Claude can see and do (module 8, page 2).
explanation.a:
is ruled
   out because the page says plainly that "the risk is not zero".
explanation.b:
Ruled out because "whatever is visible in
   them becomes part of the conversation".
explanation.c:
Ruled out because in that mode "Claude does not pause and nothing
   checks its actions".

quizzes.stem: A company approved a remote tool for Claude a year ago, and its provider has since changed hands. Which governance step was skipped?

options.a: A move to a directory connector, which needs no later review
options.b: A recheck of the whole connector list at fixed intervals
options.c: A one-time classification of the tool's data, valid while it stays in use
options.d: A switch of the tool to On demand loading in the chat

explanation.b: A change of provider is what the checklist's scheduled review exists to catch, since it says to "re-check the ones whose provider changed" (module 7, page 3).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Remote tools can change after you approve them, so install-time trust can age", wherever the connector came from.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the checklist says "Review the list on a schedule", which a one-time classification is not.
explanation.d: Ruled out because On demand is suggested "when you have ten or more connectors, so that the conversation is not crowded with tools", which is about context, not about who runs a tool.

quizzes.stem: A student submits an essay drafted entirely by Claude to a course whose rules require AI help to be declared, and does not declare it. Which Usage Policy category does this touch?

options.a: A high-risk use of the model in a regulated professional field
options.b: Fraudulent, abusive or predatory practices in the assignment
options.c: Compromising privacy or identity of the people the essay names
options.d: Misinformation spread to the public through the essay itself

explanation.b: The Usage Policy lists plagiarising or submitting AI-assisted work without proper permission or attribution under fraudulent, abusive or predatory practices (module 10, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the policy singles out "uses where output directly affects individuals or consumers".
explanation.c: Ruled out because that category covers "sharing personal information without consent".
explanation.d: Ruled out because that category is "creating or spreading misinformation, including false medical or scientific information and impersonation".

quizzes.stem: A team's bill jumps after it starts sending full-size phone photos with each request, though the text prompts are unchanged. Which two facts about images explain the jump? (Select two.)

options.a: Photos are turned into text first, which multiplies the words sent
options.b: Large pictures use many tokens, up to a model's cap
options.c: Images count toward the window but are never billed as input
options.d: Every 28 by 28 pixel square counts as one input token
options.e: Images are priced as a flat fee that ignores their size

explanation.b: Each 28 by 28 pixel patch is one visual token, so an image costs "about ceil(width/28) x ceil(height/28) tokens up to a per-model cap" (module 4, page 1).
explanation.d: Each 28 by 28 pixel patch is one visual token, so an image costs "about ceil(width/28) x ceil(height/28) tokens up to a per-model cap" (module 4, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Claude reads images and PDFs" directly, so photos are not turned into text first.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Images also cost tokens", and tokens are what is billed as input.
explanation.e: Ruled out because "A 1000 by 1000 image is 1,296 tokens", a count that depends on the size.

quizzes.stem: An analyst asks the Excel add-in to recalculate a what-if data table and to edit a VBA macro in the same workbook, and both requests fail. What explains it?

options.a: The add-in needs an Enterprise plan before it can edit macros
options.b: The workbook is too large, so Claude splits it and skips those parts
options.c: Neither is supported by this tool, so those parts stay manual
options.d: Cross-app work is switched off, which blocks edits to every sheet

explanation.c: The page lists macros and VBA, and data tables, as unsupported (module 8, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the add-ins are "installed from Microsoft AppSource, for the paid plans".
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Macros and VBA, and data tables, are unsupported".
explanation.d: Ruled out because cross-app work concerns files and uses "Let Claude work across files".

quizzes.stem: A nightly job summarises 3,000 documents. The output is good, but the bill is above budget and the run finishes after the morning deadline. Which plan fits the course's method?

options.a: Rewrite the instructions, add examples and change tier together, then compare
options.b: Move every document to the lowest tier and check a handful of summaries
options.c: Raise effort to the maximum, with fewer retries expected as a result
options.d: Name the cause, test one faster, cheaper tier on the same set, and compare

explanation.d:
The method is to diagnose first, change one thing and compare on the same inputs, and a faster lower-cost
   tier answers both the bill and the deadline.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Several simultaneous edits leave you unable to say what helped".
explanation.b:
Ruled out because "Having a good evaluation set is the most important
   step".
explanation.c:
Ruled out because effort "trades intelligence for latency and cost within a single model", and a
   maximum setting adds both.

quizzes.stem: A nightly job re-scores 200,000 different archived documents under a one-line instruction, and the results are due the next morning. Which cost lever fits best?

options.a: Batched requests, which are half the price of standard ones
options.b: Prompt cache reads, which cost a fraction of the base input price
options.c: Fast mode, which doubles the output speed at premium pricing
options.d: Higher effort, which trades latency for cost

explanation.a: Latency-tolerant bulk work suits batches, which are 50 percent cheaper (module 3, page 1).
explanation.b: Ruled out because caching pays off by "reusing context instead of resending it", and here each document is sent once under a one-line instruction, so almost nothing is resent.
explanation.c: Ruled out because fast mode offers "up to 2.5x higher output speed at premium pricing", which raises cost.
explanation.d: Ruled out because effort "trades intelligence for latency and cost within a single model", so a higher setting adds cost rather than saving it.

quizzes.stem: A support bot includes a 40,000-token manual in each turn's request, and the bill is far higher than expected. Which lever cuts that cost?

options.a: Cache that document so each later call reads it at a lower rate
options.b: Lower the output limit so each reply is cut shorter
options.c: Move to a larger context window so each long request costs less
options.d: Switch on fast mode so the turns are billed for less

explanation.a: Reusing context instead of resending it is what Projects in the apps and caching in the API are for (module 6, page 4).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "max_tokens is a cap on output, not on context", so the manual sent with each turn is still billed in full.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Larger windows raise the ceiling; they do not remove the need to decide what goes in", so the manual is still sent and paid for on each turn.
explanation.d: Ruled out because fast mode offers "up to 2.5x higher output speed at premium pricing", which raises the price.

quizzes.stem: A new labelling prompt gets about one label in four wrong, and the team's first plan is to move it to a cheaper tier to cut the bill. Which step fits?

options.a: Move to the cheaper tier now, and correct the labels in a later pass
options.b: Trim the prompt first, and expect the error rate to fall with it
options.c: Find the cause of the errors, and fix that before any cost saving
options.d: Lower the effort and change tier together, then compare the bill

explanation.c:
The labels are not yet right, so the cause is found and fixed before any cheaper setting is tried (module 6,
   page 4).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Optimisation comes after correctness: first reach the quality bar".
explanation.b:
is
   ruled out because the page lists only "a shorter prompt that keeps the same results" as a saving, not as a fix for
   errors.
explanation.d: Ruled out because with several changes at once "you do not know which change did it", and the labels are still wrong.

quizzes.stem: A shared prompt template wraps pasted contracts in `<contract>` for one author, `<doc>` for another and `<source>` for a third, and its instructions say only "the text above". Claude sometimes follows a clause inside a contract as an order. Which rule from the page fits?

options.a: Give each kind of input one meaningful label, used identically everywhere
options.b: Write the tag names in capitals to make them stand out from the text
options.c: Drop the tags and rely on the order of the sections to mark the data
options.d: Number the tags by paste, such as part1 and part2, one per item

explanation.a: One meaningfully named tag per kind of content, used the same way every time and named in the instructions, marks each contract as data (module 6, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because capitals change nothing, as "The names have no magic; they have to be meaningful and used the same way every time".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Order is not a boundary".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the rule is "One tag per kind of content".

quizzes.stem: A prompt places a 30-page policy in the middle, with the instruction to list exceptions buried in a paragraph above it. The replies often summarise instead. Which edit does the course advise?

options.a: Add several paragraphs of background to make the exceptions stand out more
options.b: Write the instruction in capital letters but keep it inside the same paragraph
options.c: Lift the instruction to the very top, ahead of the policy and all else
options.d: Set the task on a line of its own, right after the long document it concerns

explanation.d: A key instruction goes on its own line, and, as the course's working rule, the task comes after long material so that it is the last thing read (module 6, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the page says "More context is not automatically better".
explanation.b: Ruled out because the page says "A key instruction buried in a long paragraph is easy to underweight".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the page advises "Place your long documents and inputs near the top of your prompt, above your query, instructions, and examples".

quizzes.stem: A marketing lead gets a social post in the wrong tone, regenerates the same request four times, and keeps getting similar misses. What is the better method?

options.a: Regenerate the post more often and keep whichever result looks best
options.b: Rewrite the whole request from scratch each time, changing several parts together
options.c: Switch to a larger model before making any change to the brief
options.d: Change one element of the brief and compare the new reply with the last

explanation.d: Revising the request one change at a time, and comparing with the last result, is the method, and re-rolling is the reflex (module 5, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Regenerating the same request and hoping is the reflex; revising the request is the method".
explanation.b: Ruled out because the method is to "change one thing in the description", not several at once.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "The common wrong move is to change five things at once, or to reach for a bigger model".

quizzes.stem: A planner asks Claude to schedule five deliveries under several constraints and gets a wrong plan with no explanation. The planner wants to see where it went wrong, and a program reads only the final plan. Which prompt fits?

options.a: Ask the same question five times and keep the version with most agreement
options.b: Ask for the plan with a one-line reason in the field the program reads
options.c: Ask for working first, then the result after a marker for code to take
options.d: Ask for working and result mixed in one paragraph

explanation.c: Reasoning is requested before the answer and kept apart, so a program uses the answer while a person reads the steps (module 6, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Comparing detects the variation; it does not remove it".
explanation.b: Ruled out because one line is not the working, while "the steps tell you where it went wrong", and the reason would also sit in the field the program reads.
explanation.d: Ruled out because the page says to "Keep the reasoning separate from the answer".

quizzes.stem: A classifier prompt lists four allowed labels, but when a ticket fits none the model invents a fifth one. Which two changes address it? (Select two.)

options.a: Lower the temperature so the answers vary less
options.b: Spell out the closed set in the output format
options.c: Ask the model to be careful and precise
options.d: Name a fallback value for when it is unsure
options.e: Add more examples of tickets that fit the four labels

explanation.b: Say what to do when unsure, for example use unknown, and list the values as in "label is one of billing, bug, account, other" (module 6, page 2).
explanation.d: Say what to do when unsure, for example use unknown, and list the values as in "label is one of billing, bug, account, other" (module 6, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "The models this course uses do not accept them".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the page names "Stacking adjectives instead of constraints" as a trap.
explanation.e: Ruled out because "Three easy, near-identical examples teach one pattern; the model then mishandles the hard case".

quizzes.stem: A team lead asks Claude to assess whether a pilot met its targets from a set of results tables, and the replies give a general overview that never says whether each target was met. Which emphasis should the revised prompt carry?

options.a: Breadth first, many options and judgment kept for a later pass
options.b: The material, the question, the criteria and proof for each finding
options.c: Audience, tone, length and an example of the target style
options.d: Named references, claims tied to them and gaps declared in the text

explanation.b: Analysis wants the material, the question and the criteria, and the evidence for each conclusion (module 6, page 3).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the brainstorming task wants "Breadth first, many options, no early judgment".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the drafting task wants "Audience, tone, length, an example of the target style".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the research task wants "Sources named, claims tied to sources".

quizzes.stem: A prompt writer keeps moving the rule "Cite only the attached handbook, in three bullets at most" to a new place on each revision, and results wander. In the course's specification, where does that rule belong?

options.a: In the task part, folded into the verb that names the work
options.b: In the role part, written into the opening line
options.c: In the documents part, next to the handbook it governs
options.d: In the constraints part, among the conditions to be met

explanation.d: A limit on sources and a limit on length are conditions the answer must meet, which is what the constraints part answers with "What must hold?" (module 6, page 3).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the task part answers "What exactly is to be done now?".
explanation.b: Ruled out because the role part answers "Who is doing the work?".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the table files a rule such as "Use only the policy. One word." under Constraints, while the documents part answers "What material to use?".

quizzes.stem: A prompt says only "Make the tone better", and the reply is a more formal rewrite although the writer wanted it casual, and a rerun gives something different each time. Which edit to the prompt fits?

options.a: Spell out the voice intended and add one sample sentence in that style
options.b: Add background facts about the company and paste in its source material
options.c: Hand the job to a tool or a retrieval step rather than a longer prompt
options.d: Send the same request to a larger tier with a higher effort setting

explanation.a: "Better" can be read many ways and the reruns differ, which is ambiguity, and its fix is to "Say exactly what is wanted; add constraints, an example, a format" (module 6, page 4).
explanation.b: Ruled out because missing context shows as "Generic or invented content", not as a reasonable answer to the wrong question.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the wrong feature is the case where "The job needs something the prompt cannot give".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the wrong model is "Correct instructions, correct context, still a capability or speed miss", and this instruction is not yet correct.

quizzes.stem: A charity's draft appeal describes the families it serves in a pitying tone. Which check from the non-profit list applies?

options.a: Whether the wording respects the people it speaks about
options.b: Whether the appeal overstates what the programme has achieved so far
options.c: Whether the figures cited match the programme's own records
options.d: Whether donors' and families' records stay out of the draft

explanation.a: The non-profit list includes whether the language fits the community described (module 9, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because that check is "whether a draft overstates what the programme achieved".
explanation.c: Ruled out because that check is "every claim about impact, every statistic and every funder requirement against the source".
explanation.d: Ruled out because that check concerns data care, since "Donor and beneficiary records are sensitive".

quizzes.stem: A project manager asks Cowork for a one-page status pack and wants the reviewer to spot weak points quickly. Which line in the outcome description supports that?

options.a: Ask it to leave out anything uncertain, keeping the page clean
options.b: Ask it to mark each figure it failed to confirm from the sources
options.c: Ask it to rate its own confidence in each section out of ten
options.d: Ask it to add a source from memory beside each figure

explanation.b: The worked task asks it to list any figure it could not verify, so the reviewer goes straight to the weak points (module 8, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "A declared gap is information".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".
explanation.d: Ruled out because a hallucination can be "an invented citation, a function that does not exist".

quizzes.stem: Over a few exchanges, a student accepts each reframing of their thesis that Claude offers, without comparing it with their first idea. Which check from the student's list was missed?

options.a: Whether the explanation Claude gave was actually correct in each detail
options.b: Whether the rules of the course allow the amount of help that was used
options.c: Whether the tool is steering the argument to a position of its own
options.d: Whether each fact and citation in the essay has been confirmed independently

explanation.c: The student's checks include whether the tool is leading the author to a conclusion rather than helping them reach one (module 9, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because that check is "whether an explanation is actually correct", which concerns correctness.
explanation.b: Ruled out because that is "honesty about help received under the rules of their course", which concerns ownership.
explanation.d: Ruled out because that check is "every fact and citation that goes into graded work", which concerns accuracy and not direction.

quizzes.stem: A clerk sends Claude a sideways, blurry phone photo of a handwritten delivery note and enters the numbers it reports without a second look. Which concern applies?

options.a: A glance at a few figures will do, since Claude reads handwriting well
options.b: Check each figure against the paper, since such images can be misread
options.c: The figures are safe if Claude is asked to say how sure it is of each one
options.d: The figures can be trusted when they are small whole numbers

explanation.b: The vision page warns that low-quality or rotated images lead to misreadings, so a blurry, sideways photo calls for checking each reading (module 4, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the vision page says "Always carefully review and verify Claude's image interpretations".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Do not use Claude for tasks requiring perfect precision or sensitive image analysis without human oversight".

quizzes.stem: Reviewers of a research assistant's answers keep finding claims the material does not bear out, and tracing each one by hand is slow. Which prompt addition fits?

options.a: A second run of each question to compare the two answers
options.b: A score out of ten that the assistant gives to each answer it writes
options.c: A word-for-word quote backing each statement it makes
options.d: Permission to say it does not know whenever the material is thin

explanation.c: Cite and retract: a supporting quote for each claim makes every statement traceable, and the model can drop any claim it cannot support (module 1, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Comparing detects the variation; it does not remove it".
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".
explanation.d: Ruled out because that technique tells the model "it may say so when the material is not enough", and it traces nothing.

quizzes.stem: A strategist uses Research mode for a vendor comparison and receives a report with a citation after each claim. Which step is still needed before it goes to the board?

options.a: Run the same research again with web search off and compare the totals
options.b: None; every claim already has its citation
options.c: Open the cited pages behind the figures that drive the decision
options.d: Repeat the research several times and keep the statements that every run shares

explanation.c: A citation shows where an answer came from, not that the source is right, so the statements that matter are checked against it (module 7, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because Research needs "web search must be turned on".
explanation.b: Ruled out because "a citation shows where an answer came from, not that the source is right".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Comparing detects the variation; it does not remove it".

quizzes.stem: A team adds quotes, citations, an "I don't know" option and a restricted source list, and then tells users the answers no longer need review. Which two statements describe how the course treats that claim? (Select two.)

options.a: It is sound, because each technique adds an independent check in code
options.b: It overreaches, since errors are reduced and not removed
options.c: It is reasonable if users are told to ask Claude how sure it is
options.d: It is sound, because grounded prompts keep invented claims from users
options.e: It still calls for someone to verify what will drive decisions
